comparator.name: Regenerative Medicine and Technology (BSc)
comparator.academicYear: 2025-2026 (Education and Examination Regulations Bachelor Regenerative Medicine and Technology 2025-2026, Appendix 3, and the 2025-2026 programme guide; checked 2026-10-05)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s1, s2, s3, s4) describe the three-year, English-taught, full-time BSc in words only and give no EC; the curriculum page (s4) links to the programme guide and archived guides, and curriculum.maastrichtuniversity.nl was not used. The 180-EC reconstruction uses the 2025-2026 Education and Examination Regulations (s0, Article 3.6 and Appendix 3): a major of 150 EC and a minor of 30 EC, with each course year at 60 EC. Year 1 has 41 EC of six courses and 19 EC of longitudinal lines; year 2 has 38 EC of six courses, 15 EC of lab skills and academic development lines (8+5+2) and one 7-EC design-project track; year 3 has a 20-week minor of 30 EC followed by a 20-week graduation project (thesis, internship and defence) of 30 EC. The 2025-2026 programme guide (s5) supplies the course content and confirms the EC of every course. It lists RMT2006 From Research to Market Value without a description, so that component is placed from its title and the programme pages (s2, s3) only. The minor is open choice and is preserved as 30 EC of open space rather than filled with invented content. The Regulations and the programme guide are for 2025-2026, which the programme pages still publish as the latest curriculum; no 2026-2027 regulations were found, so a human may want to confirm that the 2026-2027 curriculum is unchanged. The Design Project has a clinical and a technological track of 7 EC each; the clinical track is reconstructed (see routeSelection).

routeSelection.basis: The generic bachelor has no formal specialisation, only a choice in year 2 between the Design Project clinical track (RMT2103) and technological track (RMT2104), 7 EC each. Both are equally general; the official curriculum (Appendix 3 of the Regulations and the programme guide) lists the Clinical Track first, so it is used as the neutral tie-break. The choice is independent of UCR fit and changes only 7 EC.

core: Biological and molecular foundations of regenerative medicine: biochemistry and the chemistry of life, cell biology, tissue structure and function, stem-cell potency and cell-matrix interaction (The Molecular Basis of Life; Cells: From Lab to Production)

Medical foundations: anatomy, physiology and immunology of the organ systems targeted by regenerative medicine, inflammation, foreign-body response and transplant immunology, wound healing and vascularisation (Principles of Medicine; Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine)

Regeneration and tissue repair: the intrinsic regenerative capacity of tissues, functional repair versus regeneration, ageing, and cell-based, immune-based and gene-based regenerative therapies (The Intrinsic Regenerative Capacity of the Human Body; Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine)

Engineering, physics and mathematics foundations: vectors, differential equations, mechanics of materials, rheology, thermodynamics, circuits, and the chemistry and materials science needed to design biomedical materials (Foundations of Engineering; Materials Science in Biological Applications)

Advanced regeneration technologies: biomaterials, tissue engineering, micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication (Materials Science in Biological Applications; Advanced Technologies for Regeneration)

Programming, statistics, data analysis and computational modelling: scripting, probability, regression, data-driven and differential-equation modelling and an introduction to neural networks (Coding and Data Crunching; Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems)
Laboratory skills and biomedical laboratory research: lab skills lines in years 1 and 2, experimental design, statistics for experimental data and reporting

Design, innovation and entrepreneurship: the design project lines (analysing a clinical problem, designing and marketing a new application), valorisation and market value, and the ethics of regenerative medicine applications
Academic development: self-regulated learning, professional behaviour, scientific storytelling, personal development and ethical and scientific-integrity standards (Academic Development Lines)
Research training and thesis: a 20-week individual graduation project with thesis and oral defence, preceded by a 30-EC minor
adjacent: Biomedical engineering and medical devices: engineering combined with medicine for devices and implants, with medical-device developer as a named career and biomedical engineering and imaging engineering as named further study
questions: How can the body's own repair ability be stimulated or engineered so that damaged tissue is regenerated as an alternative to organ transplantation or life-long medication?
How are scientific discoveries in regenerative medicine turned into treatments, products and ventures that reach patients?

trace: introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function and connects them to health and disease; it directly implements the biological foundation that The Molecular Basis of Life and Principles of Medicine build on, without their regenerative-medicine framing

teaches the cell biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, cell structure and physiology and current life-science methods; it directly implements the cell-biology foundation of regenerative medicine but does not cover stem-cell potency, lineage commitment or cell manufacture

studies the normal functioning of the human body, from molecular and cellular physiology through homeostasis and signalling to the integration of organ systems; it directly implements the physiology taught in Principles of Medicine

explores the chemistry of life, namely proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids, metabolic pathways and applications in medicine and biotechnology; it directly implements the biomolecular and chemical part of The Molecular Basis of Life, but it is biochemistry rather than the general, organic and physical chemistry that course also teaches

introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work on blood, bacteria, protein production and analysis, DNA isolation and bioinformatics searches and builds a foundation for biomedical research; it directly implements part of the laboratory training in the lab skills lines, although its themes do not include stem-cell culture or biomaterials work

covers cell injury and death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis and the molecular genetics of disease; it directly implements the study of tissue repair, regeneration and gene-related disease mechanisms that underlies the regenerative-capacity and therapy courses

studies the structure of the human body in relation to function through imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials, system by system; it directly implements the anatomy taught in Principles of Medicine

covers the origin, kinetics, targets, therapeutic use and toxicity of drugs and explains therapies through molecular targets and physiological consequences; it makes a specific complementary contribution to understanding the medicinal and advanced-therapy treatments that regenerative approaches complement or replace, but it contains no regenerative-medicine content

teaches innate and adaptive immune responses, recognition of self and non-self, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology; it directly implements the immunology and inflammation taught in Principles of Medicine and the immune interactions that Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine applies to implants and cell therapies, although it is not taught in a transplant or regeneration context

links normal function and pathophysiology for the cardiovascular, lung, kidney, digestive, endocrine and central nervous systems with clinical cases; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the organ systems and chronic diseases that regenerative treatments target, but it teaches disease mechanisms rather than regeneration

provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling and applies them to a case study; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the physics, mathematics and materials foundations of Foundations of Engineering, although it is framed for sustainability and not for human biomechanics

builds on Sustainability Essentials I with three topics, waves, chemistry and materials science, and a project that applies them; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the chemistry and materials-science foundations behind Materials Science in Biological Applications, but it is a sustainability course and teaches no biomaterials or cell-material interaction

introduces structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging and computational problem-solving; it directly implements the scripting and programming foundation of Coding and Data Crunching, which uses R

teaches integration, complex numbers, differential equations and equation solving; it directly implements the mathematics of differential equations and integration used in Foundations of Engineering and Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems

develops data visualisation, cleaning and manipulation on real data sets and ends with an own research project; it directly implements the data-handling, visualisation and analysis part of Coding and Data Crunching

provides the foundation of mathematical statistics: probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements the probability and statistics taught in Coding and Data Crunching at greater mathematical depth

teaches numerical methods for differential equations, root finding, interpolation, differentiation and integration with attention to accuracy and stability; it directly implements the differential-equation modelling and simulation of Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems, but without biological applications

covers regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering with real medical data; it directly implements the linear and non-linear data-driven models of Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems

teaches the design and development cycle in a team (interviewing customers, forming a product concept, developing a fabrication method, analysing costs and sustainability) with experiments, mathematical modelling and prototyping; it directly implements the team design-and-development cycle of the design project lines, although the products are consumer products and not clinical applications

teaches venture creation from ideation to pitch with design thinking, business-model development, market validation and business planning; it directly implements the entrepreneurship and market-value part of the curriculum (From Research to Market Value and the valorisation aims of the design project), without any health-care content

teaches how to plan and carry out customer and market research, analyse the findings and turn them into business ideas; it makes a specific complementary contribution to testing the market value of an innovation, but it is not specific to health care

teaches research design, operationalisation, sampling, experiments and surveys and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the experimental design, statistics and reporting of experimental data in the lab skills lines and to research training for the thesis, although it is oriented to business and behavioural research

teaches moral-reasoning theories and practical ethics including privacy, equality and future generations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the ethical debate on regenerative-medicine applications in Regenerative Medicine in Society and to the ethical and integrity standards of the academic development lines, but it has no biomedical focus

alternatives.label: Closest match to Regenerative Medicine and Technology: Biomedical Science with Engineering, Data and Innovation Foundations
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has eleven biological and medical courses (Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine, Molecular Cell Biology, Life Science Laboratory, Biochemistry, Human Physiology, Functional Anatomy, Molecular Pathology & Genetics, Pharmacology, Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease), eight engineering, mathematics and data courses (Sustainability Essentials I and II, Mathematical Methods, Computational & Numerical Methods, Introduction to Programming, Introduction to Data Science, Probability & Statistics, Machine Learning), five innovation, research-method and ethics courses (Consumer Product Design, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Market Research, Research Methods & Statistics, Ethics) and Personal & Professional Development. Biomedical science is the largest strand but only about half of the programme, and UCR has no course in regenerative medicine, biomaterials or tissue engineering, so the label names the closest match together with the engineering, data and innovation content and does not present it as a regenerative-medicine degree.
alternatives.concept: UM's Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor combines biology, chemistry and data science, engineering (mathematics, physics, materials), medicine (anatomy, physiology, immunology) and entrepreneurship to design methods that let the body repair itself, with lab skills, design projects and academic development throughout, a 30-EC minor and a graduation project. This alternative reproduces that core as closely as UCR's catalogue allows: biomolecular, cell-biological, physiological, anatomical, immunological and pathological science as the foundation for tissue repair and regeneration; the engineering, mathematics, programming, statistics and machine-learning foundations of the first two years; laboratory and research-methods training; and design, entrepreneurship and market research for the translation of discoveries into products. UCR has no course in biomaterials, tissue engineering, microfabrication or biofabrication, so the advanced regeneration technologies of the Maastricht programme remain a genuine gap.
progression: Introduction to Programming, Sustainability Essentials I and Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine open semester 1, and the biology courses that require Foundation of Life (Molecular Cell Biology, Functional Anatomy and Life Science Laboratory in semester 2; Biochemistry and Human Physiology in semester 3; Infection & Immunity in semester 4; Molecular Pathology & Genetics and Pharmacology in semester 5; Mechanisms of Disease in semester 6) follow it. Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Probability & Statistics (semester 3) and Computational & Numerical Methods (semester 4), Sustainability Essentials I precedes Sustainability Essentials II (semester 4), and Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations (semester 5) precedes Market Research (semester 6). Introduction to Data Science (semester 3) precedes Machine Learning (semester 5), and Research Methods & Statistics, which introduces experimental design, follows the laboratory course (semester 6).

selection.assessment: One UCR alternative is defensible. Alternative 1 owns the eight generator-eligible rows that describe the programme's core and its translation and entrepreneurship dimension (76 regenerative medicine, 77 how the body repairs itself, 78 combining biology, engineering and medicine, 83 cell-based therapies, 90 alternatives to organ transplantation, 96 biomedical laboratory research, 100 biotechnology and healthcare entrepreneurship and 101 turning medical research into real treatments); the support-only rows 79, 84, 85, 89 and the other curricular-topic rows strengthen its biology, immunology and wound-healing courses. Two further directions were tested. Biomedical engineering and medical devices (row 86, supported by rows 87 and 97) was rejected as not-substantively-distinct: Alternative 1 already contains the engineering, mathematics, data and design courses that UCR offers, the UCR catalogue has no biomedical-engineering, device or biomechanics course, and a separate alternative could differ only by replacing the biomedical courses with further mathematics, signal-processing and computing courses whose connection to medical devices is not evidenced, so it would share about 17 of 24 courses without a genuinely different curriculum. Tissue engineering, biomaterials and biofabrication (rows 80, 81 and 82, supported by row 88) was rejected as not-feasible: UCR has no course in biomaterials, tissue engineering, microfabrication or biofabrication, and the only materials content is in the two sustainability gateway courses that Alternative 1 already includes, so a 24-course programme could not be built without padding. The search-only rows 91 to 95, 98, 99 and 102 and 103 generated no alternative, and no row is inherited across split targets.

blocks: Biochemistry, cell biology and laboratory skills

Both treat the chemistry and molecules of life; Biochemistry teaches the structure of proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids and metabolic pathways, which is an important and identifiable part of The Molecular Basis of Life, whereas the Maastricht course also teaches general, organic, inorganic and physical chemistry and tissue structure in a regenerative-medicine context.

Both extend basic cell biology; Molecular Cell Biology gives the cell-biological foundation (cell structure, physiology and current methods) on which Cells: From Lab to Production builds, but UCR has no course on stem-cell potency, cell sources, cell manufacture or cell-biomaterial constructs, so the match is partial.

Both train laboratory skills; Life Science Laboratory teaches biochemical and molecular lab work (proteins, DNA, bacteria, blood), which is an important part of the first-year lab skills line, whereas the Maastricht line runs through the year, is aligned with all courses and includes GLP/GMP, sterile work and synthesis.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: this is an attendance component of the lab skills line and no scheduled UCR course corresponds to it.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the second-year lab skills line (cell culture, functional assays, materials and tissue work) has no UCR counterpart beyond the single laboratory course matched to the year-1 line.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: this is an attendance component of the lab skills line and no scheduled UCR course corresponds to it.
Anatomy, physiology, immunology, disease and tissue repair

Both teach the functioning of the human body; Human Physiology covers organ-system physiology, homeostasis and integration, which is the physiology part of Principles of Medicine, whereas the Maastricht course also teaches anatomy and immunology in a regenerative-medicine context with dissection practicals and patient cases.

Both address the immune system's role in regenerative approaches; Infection & Immunity teaches innate and adaptive immune responses, inflammation and tissue damage, which is an important and identifiable part of Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine (physiological and pathological inflammation and transplant immunology), but UCR does not teach cell therapy, gene therapy, implants or medical devices.

Both address tissue repair and its limits; Molecular Pathology & Genetics covers inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, which is an important and identifiable part of The Intrinsic Regenerative Capacity of the Human Body, whereas the Maastricht course is devoted to the regenerative capacity of different tissues, stem cells, ageing and the limits of regeneration.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course introduces the scope, history, 3R paradigm, applications and ethics of regenerative medicine; Ethics and the biology courses are only contextual.
Engineering, physics, chemistry and materials foundations

Both give the physics, mathematics and modelling toolkit for later applied courses; Sustainability Essentials I teaches key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science and mathematics, which is an important part of Foundations of Engineering, whereas the Maastricht course teaches vector mechanics, rheology, thermodynamics, circuits and finite-element modelling for human biomechanics.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no course in biomaterials or cell-material interaction; Sustainability Essentials II treats chemistry and materials science only in a sustainability context.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course teaches micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips or biofabrication.
Programming, statistics, data analysis and modelling

Both teach handling and analysing data with code; Introduction to Data Science teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation on real data sets, which is an important part of Coding and Data Crunching, whereas the Maastricht course also teaches scripting in R, probability and inferential statistics (covered here by Introduction to Programming and Probability & Statistics) in regenerative-medicine cases.

Both build data-driven models for biological or medical data; Machine Learning teaches linear and non-linear regression, classification and tree-based methods on real medical data, which is an important part of Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems, whereas the Maastricht course also teaches multivariable calculus, differential-equation modelling and an introduction to neural networks to predict cell-biomaterial interactions and device function.

Both teach the full design-and-development cycle in a team, from analysing a need through a concept to a fabrication method; Consumer Product Design does this for consumer products, whereas the Design Project: Clinical Track designs a regeneration project with a clinical expert and a clinical problem, so the match concerns the shared educational function and not the clinical content.

Both address turning knowledge into marketable solutions; Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations teaches venture creation, market validation and business planning, which is the market-value part of From Research to Market Value, but the programme guide gives no description of the Maastricht course and the UCR course has no health-care content.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the orientation project consists of expert interviews, site visits, journal clubs and a clinical project pitch, and no scheduled UCR course corresponds to it; the design-cycle course is matched to the year-2 design project.
Academic skills, research methods, minor and bachelor thesis

Both develop academic and personal skills; Personal & Professional Development covers personal development, critical thinking, academic writing and presenting and reflection on learning, which corresponds to the learning-skills, scientific-storytelling and personal-development domains of the Academic Development Line, whereas the Maastricht line runs through the year and also covers professional behaviour in teams.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the year-2 academic development line (including choosing electives, minor and thesis topic) has no separate UCR counterpart; Personal & Professional Development is matched to the year-1 line.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 30-EC minor is open choice and is preserved as open space; no UCR course is matched to it.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no supervised graduation project; Research Methods & Statistics supports only research design and statistics and is placed in the skills block.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of biochemistry, cell biology, physiology, immunology and the mathematics, data analysis and design foundations of biomedical science. The Maastricht University Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor additionally includes specialist work in stem cells and cell manufacture, biomaterials, micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics and organs-on-chips, tissue engineering and biofabrication, gene and cell therapies and clinical design projects with MUMC+ experts. UCR students can instead combine biomedical science with engineering, data and innovation courses, but those specialist components are not offered at the same level of depth.

The Maastricht University Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor organizes study around a fixed sequence of eight-week problem-based courses in regenerative medicine and three longitudinal lines in lab skills, design projects and academic development, followed by a 30-EC minor and a 20-week graduation project. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across courses in biomedical science, mathematics, data science, sustainability, entrepreneurship and philosophy. The UCR programme therefore covers related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the Maastricht programme course by course.
